title: Age in Dog Years
story: Your dog Max just turned 4 years old. But your friend says 'That's 28 in dog years!' Wait, what? It turns out every human year equals 7 dog years. Let's write a program that converts any age into dog years — for Max, for you, and for your whole family!
why: Real-world conversions (age, currency, temperature, distance) all use the same pattern: take a number, multiply or divide it, and you get a new number. Mastering this pattern opens up a whole world of useful calculations.
analogy: Unit conversion is like a currency exchange booth — you hand over one kind of money (human years), the booth applies a rate (×7), and hands back a different kind (dog years).
expected_output:
Taylor is 12 human years old.
That's 84 in dog years!
Mom's age in dog years: 245
try_it: Calculate dog years for everyone in your family. Then try a DIFFERENT conversion: how many months old are you? (age × 12). How many days? (age × 365). Can you convert your age into cat years? (People say 1 human year = 5 cat years for adult cats.)
tips: Store the conversion result in a variable with a descriptive name: `dog_years` tells you exactly what's inside.
You can do the math directly inside `io.print`: `io.println(age * 7)` works without a separate variable.
Pick a conversion rate and multiply — the pattern is the same whether it's years to months, feet to inches, or dollars to euros.
Use `io.print` (without `ln`) to print multiple things on the same line.
common_mistakes: Using `x` instead of `*` for multiplication: `age x 7` doesn't work — use the star `*`.
Forgetting the type annotation: `let age = 12;` works, but `let age: Int = 12;` makes it clearer that you're working with numbers.
Confusing `io.print` and `io.println`: `io.print` stays on the same line, `io.println` moves to the next line.
